lines.text: From a few struggling colonies to the world's largest economy, through revolution, civil war and the Moon. This is the story of the United States.
It begins with a great crime. For more than three centuries, millions of Africans were shipped across the Atlantic in chains to work the plantations of the Americas.
From the early sixteen hundreds, British colonies took root along the Atlantic coast, from New Hampshire down to Georgia. In time there would be thirteen of them.
The first to last was Virginia, begun at Jamestown in 1607. Tobacco, slavery and an elected assembly all grew up there together.
In 1620 the Pilgrims of the Mayflower landed further north and founded Plymouth, remembered for its compact and a harvest feast shared with the Wampanoag.
In 1706 Benjamin Franklin was born, the printer, writer and diplomat whose kite and lightning rod showed that lightning is electricity.
A generation later came George Washington, the Virginia planter who would command the revolutionary army and become the first president.
John Adams, a Massachusetts lawyer, would argue hard for independence and serve as the second president.
Thomas Jefferson would write the Declaration of Independence and, as third president, double the country's size, while enslaving people on his own estate.
James Madison, often called the father of the Constitution, would help draft the Bill of Rights and lead the nation through the War of 1812.
James Monroe, the last of the Virginia founders to be president, would warn Europe to found no new colonies in the Americas.
From the mid seventeen sixties, protests over taxes from London grew into a revolution, and the colonies began to reject British rule altogether.
Andrew Jackson, born in this time, would win the Battle of New Orleans, widen the vote for white men, and sign the Indian Removal Act.
John Quincy Adams, son of John Adams, would be the sixth president and later spend years in Congress speaking against slavery.
William Henry Harrison would become the ninth president, and die just a month after taking office.
In 1775 the shooting began. The colonies fought Britain for their independence, and with French help, they would win.
In July 1776 their leaders declared the thirteen colonies free of Britain, and set out the idea that governments exist to protect the rights of the people.
And so the United States was born, a republic that would one day grow to fifty states.
Martin Van Buren, born in the new nation, would help build the Democratic Party, and see his single term swallowed by the Panic of 1837.
In 1783 the war ended with the Treaty of Paris. Britain recognised American independence and agreed its borders.
Zachary Taylor, a career soldier, would become a hero of the war with Mexico and the twelfth president.
In 1787, in Philadelphia, the Constitution was written, dividing power between three branches. It is the oldest national constitution still in use.
John Tyler would be the first vice president to take over when a president died.
James Buchanan would be president as the Southern states began to leave the Union, just before the Civil War.
In 1791 ten amendments were added, the Bill of Rights, guarding free speech, religion, the press and fair trials.
James K. Polk would, in a single term, take the country to war with Mexico and add California and the Southwest.
Millard Fillmore would sign the Compromise of 1850, holding off the split over slavery for another decade.
In 1803 the young country bought a vast land west of the Mississippi from France, and almost doubled in size overnight.
The next year Lewis and Clark set out up the Missouri, crossed the Rockies and reached the Pacific, helped along the way by Sacagawea.
Franklin Pierce, born that same year, would back the Kansas-Nebraska Act and reopen the bitter fight over slavery in the West.
Andrew Johnson would follow Lincoln into office, clash with Congress over the South, and become the first president to be impeached.
In 1809, in a Kentucky cabin, Abraham Lincoln was born. He would lead the Union through its darkest war and free the enslaved.
In 1812 war with Britain came again, fought at sea, on the Great Lakes and along the Gulf. Borders stayed the same, but national pride grew.
Ulysses S. Grant would accept Lee's surrender at Appomattox, then as president defend the rights of the formerly enslaved.
Rutherford B. Hayes would win a disputed election and pull federal troops out of the South, ending Reconstruction.
Chester A. Arthur would sign the law that began the modern civil service.
From 1830 the Cherokee, Choctaw, Seminole and other nations were forced from their homelands in the Southeast. Thousands died on the long march west.
In those same years a secret network of routes and helpers led enslaved people north to freedom, in the free states and in Canada.
James A. Garfield would be shot just four months into his presidency.
Benjamin Harrison, grandson of William Henry Harrison, would serve one term between the two of Grover Cleveland.
Grover Cleveland would be the first president to win two terms that did not follow one another.
William McKinley would lead the war with Spain in 1898, and be assassinated early in his second term.
In 1846, after the annexation of Texas, war broke out with Mexico. Mexico lost about half its land, including California.
Thomas Edison, born in 1847, would fill a laboratory at Menlo Park with inventions, from the phonograph to the electric light.
In 1848 gold was found at Sutter's Mill, and hundreds of thousands rushed to California. San Francisco boomed, and Native peoples suffered.
Woodrow Wilson would take the country into the First World War and dream of a League of Nations.
William Howard Taft would be both president and Chief Justice, the only person ever to hold the two offices.
Theodore Roosevelt would break up the great trusts, protect millions of acres of wild land, and start work on the Panama Canal.
In 1861 eleven Southern states broke away to defend slavery, and formed the Confederacy, with its capital at Richmond.
The Civil War followed, four years of fighting between North and South. The Union held, and slavery came to an end.
In 1863 Lincoln declared the enslaved free in the rebel states. The war became a war for freedom, and Black men joined the Union army.
That summer, at Gettysburg in Pennsylvania, the Union turned back Lee's invasion of the North in three bloody days.
Then came Reconstruction, the attempt to rebuild the South and give the freed people citizenship and the vote.
In 1865 the Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery throughout the land.
Warren G. Harding, born that year, would one day promise Americans a return to normal life after the First World War.
In 1869 the rails met at Promontory Summit in Utah. A journey of months across the continent now took about a week.
Calvin Coolidge, a man of few words, would govern through the roaring boom of the twenties.
Herbert Hoover, an engineer, would be in the White House when the stock market crashed.
Franklin D. Roosevelt would be elected four times, fight the Depression with the New Deal, and lead the nation through most of the Second World War.
Harry S. Truman would order the atomic bombings of Japan, launch the Marshall Plan, and send troops to Korea.
In 1886 a gift from France rose in New York harbour: the Statue of Liberty, holding her torch over the ships of arriving immigrants.
Dwight D. Eisenhower would plan the D-Day landings and later serve as the thirty-fourth president.
From 1892 millions of newcomers passed through Ellis Island, the gateway where Europe's emigrants first set foot in America.
Ernest Hemingway, born in 1899, would change the way English is written, with short, plain sentences.
Walt Disney would create Mickey Mouse, make the first feature-length cartoon, and open Disneyland in California.
In December 1903, at Kitty Hawk, the Wright brothers made the first powered, controlled flights. The longest lasted under a minute.
Lyndon B. Johnson would sign the Civil Rights and Voting Rights Acts, while the war in Vietnam darkened his years.
In 1908 came Ford's Model T, cheap and tough. Built on a moving assembly line, it put ordinary families on the road.
Ronald Reagan, the Hollywood actor turned president, would cut taxes, build up the military, and meet Gorbachev as the Cold War waned.
Richard Nixon would open relations with China, and become the only president to resign.
Rosa Parks would refuse to give up her bus seat in Montgomery, and help start a year-long boycott.
Gerald Ford would take office when Nixon resigned, the only president never elected as president or vice president.
In 1914 war engulfed Europe. The United States would join in 1917, and the old empires would fall.
John F. Kennedy, born in 1917, would face down the Cuban missiles, set the goal of the Moon, and be killed in Dallas.
In 1920 alcohol was banned across the country. Prohibition fed gangsters and speakeasies, and was finally repealed in 1933.
George H. W. Bush would be president as the Cold War ended, and lead the coalition in the Gulf War.
Jimmy Carter, a peanut farmer from Georgia, would broker peace between Egypt and Israel at Camp David.
In 1929 Martin Luther King Junior was born. He would lead the civil rights movement and dream aloud at the March on Washington.
That October, prices on Wall Street collapsed. Years of boom ended in a few days of panic.
The Great Depression followed. Millions lost their jobs and homes, and the government took on new work to help them.
Neil Armstrong, born in 1930, would be the first person to walk on the Moon.
Elvis Presley would blend country, blues and gospel, and become the face of rock and roll.
In 1939 the Second World War began. It would leave the United States one of two superpowers.
On the seventh of December 1941, Japanese planes struck Pearl Harbor in Hawaii. The next day, America was at war.
Muhammad Ali, born in 1942, would be world heavyweight champion three times, and refuse to fight in Vietnam.
That same year Joe Biden was born. He would spend decades in the Senate and become the forty-sixth president.
Donald Trump, born in 1946, would go from real estate and television to the presidency, twice.
George W. Bush, son of a president, would lead the country through the September attacks and the wars that followed.
Bill Clinton would preside over a long boom and a balanced budget, and survive impeachment.
In 1954 the Supreme Court ruled that separate schools for Black and white children were unequal, and so unlawful.
Steve Jobs, born in 1955, would co-found Apple and bring the personal computer, and later the iPhone, to millions.
Bill Gates would co-found Microsoft, whose software ran most of the world's personal computers.
That year the war in Vietnam began. The United States would be drawn deep into it, and leave two decades later.
Michael Jackson would begin as a child star and make Thriller, among the best-selling albums ever.
In 1961 Barack Obama was born. He would become the first Black president of the United States.
In October 1962 Soviet missiles were found in Cuba. For thirteen days the world stood at the edge of nuclear war.
In 1964 the Civil Rights Act banned discrimination by race, religion or sex, the movement's great legal victory.
And in July 1969 Apollo 11 landed on the Moon. Neil Armstrong stepped out onto its surface.
In 1972 a break-in at the Democrats' offices grew into the Watergate scandal, and two years later Nixon resigned.
In 1991 the World Wide Web arrived, and America led the world into the internet age.
On the eleventh of September 2001, hijacked planes struck New York and the Pentagon. Nearly three thousand people were killed.
In 2003 American forces invaded Iraq and toppled Saddam Hussein, followed by years of insurgency.
In 2005 Hurricane Katrina broke the floodwalls of New Orleans. Much of the city drowned, and the slow response angered the nation.
In 2007 Apple unveiled the iPhone, and put a computer in every pocket.
Then house prices fell, and a banking crisis spread around the world. Lehman Brothers failed, and governments rushed to rescue the rest.
In 2020 the COVID pandemic arrived, bringing lockdowns, closed schools and vaccines made at record speed.
That spring, George Floyd was killed by a Minneapolis police officer, and protests against racism swept the country and the world.
On the sixth of January 2021, a mob stormed the Capitol, trying to stop Congress from certifying the election.
In late 2022 ChatGPT was released, reaching a hundred million users in about two months, and the race for artificial intelligence was on.
And in 2026 the United States shared the World Cup with Canada and Mexico, the first with forty-eight teams.
Two and a half centuries on, the American story is still being written.
